activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Cats cannot make enough of their own taurine, a nutrient found in meat, and a lack of it can cause heart disease and blindness.
story:
Caleb's family had finally said yes to a pet, and on Saturday morning he stood in the pet store with a folded list in his pocket. The kitten was already chosen, a gray one asleep in a carrier by the register, but the food aisle had stopped him cold. Dog food and cat food filled opposite shelves, in bags that looked almost the same. "Why is it all separate?" he asked. "It's just kibble."

His friend Thiago, who had come along to help carry things, shrugged. "My uncle says cats can't make enough of their own taurine. It's a nutrient in meat, and if they don't get it they can get heart disease and go blind."

Caleb picked up a bag of dog food anyway, because it was three dollars cheaper and twice the size. Then he put it back. A cat going blind because he saved three dollars was not a trade he wanted to make, even if the money was coming out of his allowance.

At home, the kitten hid behind the couch for the first hour, and the real problem began. The list said to feed her, but the list didn't say how to get a scared cat to eat. Caleb set the bowl down, backed away, and watched. She didn't move. He tried again closer to her, and she still didn't move, though her ears turned toward the bowl when the kibble rattled. That gave him an idea. She wasn't refusing food, she was refusing distance. If the bowl scared her, maybe the food itself could be moved to her instead of the other way around. He took a single piece of kibble and rolled it slowly along the floor, so it stopped just past her whiskers, where she could reach it without leaving her hiding spot. She ate it. He rolled another. She ate that too.

The kitten, whom he had named Pip, still wouldn't come out, but by evening she was eating from a shallow dish that he had pushed halfway under the couch. He wrote this down in a notebook, the way he did for science class, in case the pattern stopped working. Then he thought of a problem he couldn't see. If Pip ate only what she could reach under the couch, she might eat too little, and a cat who ate too little meat wouldn't get enough taurine either, no matter what the bag said. He couldn't watch her all night to find out.

So he set up an experiment. He borrowed his dad's old magnifying lens, propped his phone above the dish on a stack of books, and aimed the lens so the camera could magnify the bowl from across the room. If there was less food by morning, she had eaten when no one was near. He wrote "amendment to plan: check recording at breakfast" on the list his mom had made, and stuck it to the fridge.

On Sunday the kitchen smelled like toast and like his neighbor Ms. Becker, who had come over with a blanket she said every new cat needed. Caleb showed them the recording. At one in the morning, a gray shape crept out, ate for four full minutes, and crept back. Ms. Becker voted the video excellent. His dad voted it excellent. Thiago, watching over video chat, voted excellent too. It was unanimous. Caleb slid the dish a few inches farther from the couch, not too far, just enough to be a small step forward, and pressed record again.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about something that will happen later, often noticed only on a second reading.
story:
Addison had read "The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter" once already, and she had hated the ending. Now she sat cross-legged in the reading nook behind the living room couch, her back against the wall, the story open on her knees like she was about to excavate something buried in it.

Ms. Petrov had written one comment in red pen at the bottom of Addison's quiz: "Look for the hints. Reread." That was all. Addison had stared at it for two days, because hints about what? The story seemed simple. A girl named Marta rows out to check the lamp, a storm rolls in, and then, on the last page, the boat is gone and Marta is standing on the rocks, soaked, holding something in her fist. The something was never described. Ms. Petrov had asked the class what Marta held, and Addison had written "a fishhook," which had earned her the red comment instead of a checkmark.

Jada dropped onto the couch above the nook, peering over the back cushion. "You're reading it again? It wasn't even good."

"It was good," Addison said. "Something's hidden in it." She flipped back to page one and started over, slower this time, dragging her finger under each line. On page one, the keeper, Marta's father, winds the lamp mechanism and says the lamp "turns like a slow revolution," and Marta notices a loose screw on the lens housing. Addison's finger stopped. A loose screw. She read the last page again. The lamp had failed in the storm, and a ship had wrecked on the rocks, and Marta was standing there holding something small and metal in her fist.

Her heart started going fast. "Jada. The screw."

"What screw?"

"On page one. The lamp had a loose screw, and nobody tightened it, and then the lamp failed." She checked the middle of the story to be sure. The father says he'll fix it "tomorrow," which in a storm story is like a character saying everything is fine. Addison wrote both clues on a sticky note, then wrote her answer underneath: Marta is holding the screw. The thing that sank the ship is the thing in her hand.

"That's what foreshadowing is, right?" Jada said, squinting at the page. "A hint early on about what happens later. You only catch it the second time through."

Addison hadn't known the word before that moment, and now it felt like a key that fit a lock. She pushed the sticky note into her pocket, grabbed her quiz, and slid out of the nook so fast she banged her knee on the coffee table. The pain was temporary. Ms. Petrov's classroom was four blocks away, and school let out in twenty minutes.

"Where are you going?" Jada called.

"To find out if I'm right," Addison shouted, already pulling on her shoes at the door.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Repeating an experiment several times and averaging the results reduces the effect of random errors in any single trial.
story:
Charles stomped into the backyard carrying his water balloon launcher, which was really just a sling made of surgical tubing lashed between two fence posts. His problem was simple: for the science fair he had to claim how far the launcher could shoot, and yesterday's single test had gone forty-two feet, which felt like a lucky fluke. Today he wanted to know the truth.

Jersey was already sitting on the picnic table with a clipboard, because Jersey liked clipboards more than he liked most people. "Ready," Jersey said. "Trial one."

Charles pulled the balloon back to the knot he had tied in the tubing, let go, and watched the balloon sail over the compost bin and splat against the far fence. Jersey paced it out and marked the distance. Trial two went barely half as far. Trial three flew sideways and exploded on the bird bath.

"That's weird," Charles said, pulling the tubing taut and checking the knot. "I did the same thing every time. Same balloon weight, same stretch."

"Maybe the wind," Jersey said, squinting up. "Or maybe the balloon rolls a little before it settles." Alan leaned over the fence from next door and offered his opinion, which was that the launcher was volatile, since it never did the same thing twice.

Charles thought about that while he reloaded. A single launch couldn't be trusted, because any one throw could be thrown off by something tiny, a gust, a wobble in the tubing, his own fingers slipping. But if he repeated the experiment and averaged all the results together, the weird ones would cancel out and he would get a number he could actually defend at the fair. He could even replicate the whole test tomorrow to check it.

"Let's run it ten times," he said. "Then we average."

They spent the next hour launching, pacing, and recording. One balloon cleared the fence entirely and earned a whoop from Alan, who climbed down from his fence to help refill the bucket. Two landed short and sad. When they finally added the distances and divided, the average came out to thirty-one feet, which was less than his lucky forty-two but steady.

Mr. Rajapakse, watering his tomatoes on the other side of the hedge, called over, "You boys have been at that all afternoon. What did you learn?"

"That one launch means nothing," Charles said, holding up the clipboard, "but ten launches tell the truth."

He turned back to the fence posts, loaded another balloon, and pulled the tubing back to the knot. "Trial eleven," he announced. "Just to be sure."

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: The three points in an argument must be truly different reasons; if two points say the same thing in different words, the argument really has only two.
story:
Gabriel sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with a chrome napkin dispenser on one side and his essay packet on the other. The assignment was due Monday, and Ms. Delgado had been firm about it: no drafting until every student had a thesis statement and three points written out. Gabriel had a thesis. He had three points. The trouble was that something about them felt off, like a picture hung slightly crooked, and he couldn't see which way to straighten it.

"You look like you're solving a mystery," his grandfather said, setting down two glasses of lemonade. He had been a printer for forty years and could spot a crooked line from across a room.

"I sort of am." Gabriel slid the paper across the table. "My thesis is that the school should let kids keep phones in their lockers instead of banning them completely. Point one is that phones help kids contact parents after school. Point two is that phones are useful in emergencies. Point three is that a kid might need to reach his mom or dad in a hurry."

His grandfather read it twice, tapping the table with one finger. "Huh," he said. That was all, which Gabriel had learned was often a lot.

He called Cadence, because Cadence could argue with a fence post and win. She answered on the second ring, and Gabriel read his outline out loud while she drew something on her end, the sound of her pencil scratching through the speaker.

"Stop," she said. "Go back to two and three." He read them again. "Those are the same reason wearing different clothes. If two points say the same thing in different words, the argument really has only two. You've got an emergency point twice."

Gabriel stared at his paper. She was right, and it was strange how the sameness had been invisible until she said it, like a pattern hidden in a random-seeming wallpaper that suddenly resolves into flowers once you see it. He crossed out point three and sat there with the empty space. What was a third reason that didn't correspond to the first two?

He wandered into the living room, where his grandfather's old filing cabinet held the manual for everything in the house, including the toaster and the furnace, each one with its warranty stapled to the front page. Gabriel leafed through them without really meaning to, and then he stopped. The manuals listed reasons in neat numbered sections, and each numbered section was a genuinely different thing: safety, upkeep, parts.

"Grandpa," he called, "how do you decide what goes in a new section?"

"Anything that's its own reason gets its own number," his grandfather called back. "If it's just the last section said again, it doesn't get one."

Gabriel went back to the kitchen table. He wrote a new point three: kids would be more likely to follow a fair rule than a total ban, so lockers would cause fewer confiscations. Then he read all three points in order, listening for that crooked-picture feeling. It was gone. He circled the outline twice, packed it in his backpack, and carried his lemonade out to the porch, where the evening was just starting to cool.

"Cadence," he said, texting her one-handed, "if my next argument only has two real points, I'm making you find it before I do."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: When viewing a slide, you start with the lowest-power objective lens to find and focus on the cells before switching to higher power.
story:
Jordan had been waiting all week for the microscope lab, and now he was stuck with a gray smear where onion cells were supposed to be. He twisted the focus knob back and forth, but nothing sharpened. Across the table, Lily-Anne was already sketching little brick-shaped cells into her lab sheet.

"What power are you on?" she asked, leaning over.

"Forty times. The big one." Jordan sat back and exhaled slowly through his nose. "I cranked it to the strongest lens so I could see everything at once. All I get is blur."

Lily-Anne tapped his objective turret, the little rotating wheel that held the three lenses. "Try the smallest one first," she said. "That's how Darwin did it. Find the cells down there, get them sharp, and then switch up."

Jordan turned the turret until the shortest lens clicked into place. He bent over the eyepiece, and there they were: rows of cells like a honeycomb, pale and tidy. He worked the coarse knob in tiny increments until the edges crisped up, then flipped to the next lens. The cells jumped closer, already almost in focus.

"Mr. Rahman," Jordan called, raising his hand. The teacher wandered over, and Jordan pointed at his labeled diagram. "The dark blob in the middle, that's the nucleus, right? And the outer line is the cell wall?"

"Wall on the outside, membrane just inside it," Mr. Rahman said. "Draw the membrane as a second line, thin one. Check the board if you're unsure of the order."

Jordan drew the second line carefully, then hesitated. He glanced at Darwin's side of the table, where Darwin was squinting into his scope with the same defeated look Jordan had worn five minutes ago.

"Start with the lowest-power objective," Jordan told him quietly. "Find them there first, then go up." Darwin rotated the turret, and a second later his shoulders dropped in relief.

"One factor I didn't count on," Jordan said, filling in the last label, "was that the strongest lens would be the hardest one to find anything with."

Lily-Anne slid the box of prepared slides toward him. "There's a rebellious one in there, a cheek cell slide somebody made crooked. Want to try it before the bell?"

Jordan clicked the slide onto the stage and started, as always now, at low power.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox, because it is linked to Reye's syndrome, a rare but serious illness affecting the liver and brain.
story:
Stella sat at the kitchen table on day four of the flu, wrapped in a blanket, staring at the medicine cabinet through the doorway. Her head ached, her fever had finally dropped, but her whole body felt like it had been squeezed through a rolling pin. She wanted something for the ache, and she wanted it before her mom got home.

She padded to the cabinet on cold feet and opened it. Cough syrup, a thermometer, a box of bandages, and there, a bright orange bottle of aspirin. She reached for it, then paused. Taped inside the cabinet door was a folded note in her mother's handwriting. Stella pulled it free and read it.

"Do not give this to Stella when she has the flu. Ask Mr. Bui if you're not sure why." The note was old, from two years ago, when the neighbor had helped out during a bad flu season. Stella frowned. Aspirin was just pain medicine, wasn't it? Why would it matter whether you had the flu or a headache? She felt a flicker of resentment at being told what to do through a sticky note instead of an actual conversation, and an almost equal urge to take two pills anyway. She was twelve, not a baby. But the note was specific, and her mother was never specific without a reason.

She put the bottle back and knocked on the wall beside the phone. Mr. Bui answered on the second ring, the way he always did, as if he had been waiting by the phone for someone to call about medicine labels or tomato plants or the weather. "Mr. Bui, it's Stella. Can you come over for a minute? I have a question about aspirin."

He arrived in his garden clogs ten minutes later, carrying a small paper bag of oranges that always seemed to accompany him on his visits. Stella showed him the note and the bottle. "I'm not going to take it without asking," she said, "but I want to understand why. Is it because kids are smaller? Like a dose thing?"

"Not a dose thing," Mr. Bui said. He set the oranges on the counter and turned the bottle to read the back, though Stella suspected he already knew what it said. "Children and teenagers should not take aspirin during flu or chickenpox. It's linked to something called Reye's syndrome." He handed the bottle back. "Rare, but serious. Liver and brain."

"Reye's syndrome," Stella repeated slowly, turning the word over. Rare, but serious, and it involved the liver and brain. So the problem wasn't how much you took, it was when. The same pill that was fine for a headache on a healthy day was off-limits on a flu day. She thought of other medicines in the cabinet. Did they have the same rule? She checked the cough syrup label, then the small box of children's pain reliever in the drawer. No aspirin listed. That, she decided, was probably the point.

Mr. Bui pointed at the kettle. "While you're being a scientist, make tea. For me, and for you." Stella filled the kettle and set it on the burner. On the counter lay her phone, and she picked it up and typed a message to Tatiana, who was home with the same flu: "Did you know we can't have aspirin when we have the flu? Something called Reye's syndrome. Liver and brain. Check your cabinet." The reply came back in under a minute: "We only have the orange pills too. Dhruv is bringing soup tomorrow, I'll warn him."

The kettle began to whistle. Stella poured two cups and carried them to the table, and Mr. Bui peeled one of his oranges in a single long spiral and set half of it on a saucer beside her cup. The steam rose between them, and the spiral of peel curled on the counter like a small bright rope.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A symbol is an object, person or event that stands for an idea beyond itself, and a reader must support any meaning they give it with details from the story.
story:
The bell over the bookshop door jingled, and Thomas hurried past the shelves of mystery novels toward the back table where the Saturday book club met. Mr. Quinn, who owned the shop, was already setting out chairs, and the clock above the register read 2:41. The discussion started at three, and Thomas had not finished his homework.

"You look like a boy being chased," said Mr. Quinn.

"I have to explain the story to everyone, and I don't get it. There's this red door, and Kaydence says it means danger, and Declan says that's made up, and I have to decide who's right. By three o'clock." Thomas dropped his copy of the story on the table, a thin stapled packet with a dog-eared corner. He had read it twice on the bus and still felt like he was groping around in a dark room.

Mr. Quinn straightened a chair. "Read me the part about the door."

Thomas found the page. The first mention came early, when the main character noticed the red door at the end of the hall and thought it looked out of place, like a warning light in a house that had gone quiet. Then it appeared again when the character's little brother was told never to open it. Then, near the end, on the night of the storm, the door stood slightly open, and cold air propelled the curtains across the floor like reaching hands.

"There," Thomas said, tapping the page. "It's not just one time. The author keeps bringing it up, and every time, something feels wrong."

Declan arrived with Kaydence right behind him, both of them carrying paper cups from the café next door. Kaydence sat down and slid the story toward herself. "I told you, the red door means danger."

"You said it, but you didn't prove it," Declan said. His skepticism was quiet but fixed, the way he held his cup without drinking. "I could say the door means Christmas and it would be just as true."

Thomas raised his hand, then felt silly and put it down. "Kaydence, why danger? Not because you feel it. Because of the words."

She frowned and flipped back to the first page. She read aloud slowly: "Like a warning light in a house that had gone quiet." Then she found the brother, then the storm, then the reaching hands. "It says warning. It keeps showing up when something bad is about to happen. That's three separate places."

"So the door isn't just a door," Thomas said, working it out as he spoke. "It's a symbol, an object that stands for an idea beyond itself. And you can't just announce that. You have to show the details from the story, or it doesn't count."

Declan turned his cup around once, then nodded. "Three details is significant. I'll take it."

Mr. Quinn checked the clock, which now read 2:58, and pulled the table into the center of the chairs. "Two minutes," he said. "Who's starting us off?"

"Kaydence," Thomas said. "Open to page one."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, was the first U.S. state law requiring that a young athlete with a suspected concussion be removed from play until a health professional clears them.
story:
Lydia had taped a schedule to her bedroom wall two weeks before soccer tryouts, and every afternoon since, her backyard had turned into a training field. Cones marked dribbling lanes across the grass, and the laundry line served as a crossbar. Last summer she had been cut in the first round because her passes generated no pressure on defense; this year she intended to be the player who couldn't be ignored.

Anton came over every day too, because a scout from the district team was supposed to watch tryouts, and Anton wanted that scout to remember his name. He practiced shooting until his sneakers were dark with dew. "One goal," he kept saying. "One clean goal and I'm on that list."

On the final afternoon before tryouts, they played a small scrimmage against Nyah and Lydia's older brother. Anton went up for a header, collided with the brother's shoulder, and landed hard on the packed dirt near the fence. He got up slowly, blinking, one hand pressed to his temple. "I'm fine," he said immediately. "Don't sub me out. I need the touches."

Lydia remembered something then, a flashback from the clinic waiting room last winter, when she sat with a sprained wrist. A poster on the wall had described a law about young athletes and head injuries. She hadn't paid much attention at the time, but she remembered the shape of it: a player who might have a concussion couldn't just decide to keep playing.

"Anton, sit down," she said. He protested, so she ran inside, found the flyer her brother had brought home from his league, and read it while Nyah kept the ball away from him. She carried it back out. "It's called the Zackery Lystedt Law," she read. "Washington passed it in 2009, and it was the first state law requiring a young athlete with a suspected concussion to be removed from play until a health professional clears them."

"That's for real games," Anton said, but he sat. His eyes didn't track the ball the way they had, and when Nyah tossed it to him gently, he misjudged it by a foot. Lydia watched that happen twice more and thought, that's the evidence. The rule made sense precisely because the injury was invisible; you couldn't trust a player's own word about his own head.

Something loosened in her chest, the guilt she'd felt about ruining his last practice. "If you're honest today," she told him, "maybe you miss tryouts and maybe you don't. But if you hide it and collapse at tryouts, you definitely miss the whole season." Anton looked at the ball under Nyah's foot for a long moment.

"Okay," he said. "Call my mom. And Lydia?" He managed half a grin. "Score one for me tomorrow."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The word algebra comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
story:
Julia sat at the kitchen table with her math booklet open to page 47, and the problem stared back at her like a locked door: 3x + 4 = 19. She had to solve for x, whatever that meant. Her dad had said algebra would come in seventh grade, but Ms. Zhu's class was starting early, and Julia did not want to be the one who raised her hand to say she was lost.

Finnley dropped into the chair across from her and slid over a bag of pretzels. "Stuck too?"

"Totally stuck." Julia tapped her pencil against the page. "It's like x is hiding behind everything else. I can't see it. I just have to guess what number it is."

Finnley shrugged. "Guessing got me a C minus on the practice sheet."

Julia frowned at the equation. If x was hiding, then maybe the trick was to take things away until it showed itself. She wrote 3x + 4 = 19 again on a fresh piece of paper. "What if I take away four from the left side? Then it's just 3x equals something."

"Then it's wrong," Finnley said. "You can't just do it to one side. That's like cutting one cookie in half and not the other."

Julia paused. That actually made sense. If both sides were equal, they were like two identical piles, and whatever she did to one pile she had to do to the other. She wrote 3x + 4 - 4 = 19 - 4, and underneath it, 3x = 15. Her heart beat faster. The door was opening.

"So x has to be five," she said, dividing both sides by three. "Because three fives make fifteen." She checked it: 3 times 5, plus 4, equaled 19. She actually shouted, and the dog barked from the other room.

Finnley grabbed the pencil and tried the next one, 2x - 6 = 10, adding six to both sides and then dividing. "It's like a game where every move has to happen twice," Finnley said. "This might actually be fun."

Julia was supposed to do a short history paragraph for the same class, so she looked up the word algebra on her mom's phone while the kitchen grew tranquil in the late afternoon light. She read the entry twice, then laughed out loud.

"What?" Finnley leaned over.

"Algebra comes from al-jabr," Julia read. "It was part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi."

"So the whole subject is named after a book title?"

"A thousand-year-old book title." Julia copied the fact onto her notepad, feeling like she'd solved another hidden equation. "And he probably had pretzels too." Finnley threw one at her, and she caught it in her mouth.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Telling a trusted adult is not tattling when the goal is to protect someone from harm rather than to get someone in trouble.
story:
The party was in full swing by the time Jeremy skidded through Ophelie's back gate, still holding the half-eaten granola bar he'd grabbed on the way. Streamers sagged from the umbrella stand, somebody's little brother was trying to trade his slice of cake for a puppy, and a piñata shaped like a dragon dangled from the basketball hoop. Jeremy loved piñatas. He'd been thinking about this one for three days.

Then he spotted Rhea sitting alone on the porch steps, arms wrapped around her knees. That was weird, because Rhea was usually the loudest person at any party. Last summer she had led a whole beach cleanup and made up a song about seaweed that got stuck in everyone's head for a week. Now she was staring at a spot on the concrete like it owed her money.

Near the drinks table, two kids from another class were giggling behind their cups. "Nice jacket, Rhea," one of them called out in a squeaky voice. "Did your grandma inherit it from a scarecrow?" The other one cracked up so hard he nearly spilled his juice. Rhea hunched lower.

Jeremy's stomach did a slow flip. A memory flashed back to fourth grade, when kids had called him "gullible" for weeks because he'd believed a story about a homework-eating locker monster, and nobody had said a word to stop it. He'd told the teacher on day one, and a kid named Douglas had called him a snitch, and Jeremy had spent the rest of the year wishing he'd stayed quiet. Or had he? He chewed on that old moment like gum. The teacher had stopped it, sure. But Douglas had been mad. So had telling been worth it, or had it just made things worse? He couldn't see the answer directly, so he decided to run a small test. He walked over to the drinks table, poured two cups of punch, and said loudly, "Did you know the whole thing about the locker monster was my idea? I told him that story on purpose. He fell for it because he's the most trusting kid in school, not because he's dumb." The gigglers blinked. It was even true, mostly.

Then Jeremy carried the second cup of punch over to the porch steps and sat down beside Rhea. "Dragon piñata in twenty minutes," he said. "I've been training." He mimed a batting stance. "My form is flawless. I've watched four videos." Rhea snorted, which was close to a laugh. "They've been doing that all week," she said quietly. "At school too. Every single day." Jeremy felt his jaw tighten. A one-time joke was one thing. Every day was a machine with a hinge, and it would keep swinging unless somebody jammed it.

"Hey, Mr. Nguyen?" Mr. Nguyen lived next door and was helping run the grill, flipping burgers with the focus of a brain surgeon. Jeremy pulled him aside. "Is it tattling if we tell you about it?" "Depends," Mr. Nguyen said, eyebrows up, spatula pausing. "Are you trying to get somebody in trouble, or trying to keep somebody safe?" Jeremy turned that over, and it clicked like a locker snapping shut. "Keep somebody safe," he said. "Definitely." "Then it's not tattling. Come on." Mr. Nguyen set down the spatula and walked over to the drinks table, and Jeremy watched him speak to the two kids in a low, calm voice, the kind that made backs straighten on its own.

Ten minutes later Rhea was first in line for the piñata, holding the bat like a knight's sword. The dragon swung, she spun blindfolded, and on her third swing she connected with a whump that sent candy hailing across the lawn. Kids dove everywhere. Rhea pulled off the blindfold, cheeks pink, and shoved a fistful of lollipops into Jeremy's hands. "You get the green ones," she said. "Those are clearly the best ones, and I'm not being generous, I'm being correct." Jeremy bit into a green lollipop and grinned around it.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break.
story:
Edouard sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field, his right arm resting in a white cast that ended just past his elbow. He had broken it three weeks ago falling off the goal frame during warm-ups, and today was the first day he had come back to watch practice. Grey and Adem jogged over during the water break, grass stuck to their shins.

"Mr. Wright said you can keep score for us," said Grey, handing him the clipboard. Edouard took it with his left hand. The whistle blew and the drill started again, cones and shadows stretching long across the field in the late afternoon light.

Adem flopped down beside him. "My grandpa broke his wrist in the winter. He still has his cast on. Six more weeks, the doctor said." He picked at a thread on his sock. "You got yours off in four, right?"

"That's what the doctor said," Edouard said. He watched the ball move down the field, then looked at his cast again. "Same kind of break, though. I saw the picture of it. A line across the bone, just like his." Something about it bothered him, the way a vague shape at the edge of a room bothers you until you turn and see what it is. Two breaks, the same kind, and two very different times in a cast.

He turned it over all through the scrimmage. At dinner that night he asked his mother to write it out for him, since his own writing looked like ants had walked through ink. He dictated while she printed: Dear Grandpa Adem, sorry about your wrist. Mine comes off next week. Yours is on until the summer. Why? We both broke the same bone. Write back if you figure it out. From Edouard. He read it twice, put it in an envelope, and set it by the door.

The answer came on Sunday, on a card in his grandfather's careful handwriting. The doctor told me young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break. I asked him twice to be sure. He says my bones are old and stubborn, like me. Eat well and come visit.

Edouard read it standing in the kitchen, then read it again. He got a piece of paper and wrote out the little equation of it, not with numbers but with words: young bones, faster healing, shorter cast. Then he tested it, in his own way. He called Adem. "Your cousin broke her ankle last year, she's our age. How long was her cast on?" Six weeks, Adem said, and her father had broken his ankle the year before that and been in one for nearly three months. The pattern held. It was like a rule the body followed that nobody had bothered to tell him until now.

The next practice, Mr. Wright waved him over during the cool-down. "How's the arm?"

"Off next Thursday," Edouard said. "I'm going to consume an entire pizza that night, with two hands." Mr. Wright laughed. On the field the last players were collecting the cones, and the light had gone soft and gold, and Edouard bounced the ball once on his knee, then twice, catching it under his good arm before anyone could shout at him.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: Hindus usually cremate the dead, returning the body to the five elements, though young children and some holy people are traditionally buried instead.
story:
Victor had never been inside a temple before, and the shoe rack by the door surprised him more than the incense did. He lined his sneakers beside Dan's and followed the crowd into the hall, where his neighbour Ms. Singh was waiting. "Stay close," she said quietly. "We're here for my uncle."

The ceremony moved slowly, with bells and Sanskrit that Victor could not follow, and he found himself watching the family instead. The body lay wrapped in cloth, garlanded with marigolds. When the priest spoke, Ms. Singh translated only one line: "The fire returns him to the five elements." Afterward, outside, the family carried the body toward the cremation ground, and Victor understood, with a small cold feeling, that there would be no grave to visit.

He thought of his grandmother's funeral two years ago, at the church across town. Dan had been there. They had stood at the cemetery in their stiff clothes while the coffin went down into the earth, and the pastor had talked about resurrection and heaven. Victor had imagined his grandmother somewhere above the clouds, still wearing her elastic-waisted gardening pants, still humming. It had comforted him then, though now he wondered whether he had believed it or just wanted to.

"Everyone gets burned?" he asked Ms. Singh on the drive home, and immediately worried it was rude. She shook her head. "Not the little ones," she said. "Young children are buried. Some holy people, too." She did not say why, and Victor, remembering his manners, did not press. But the fact snagged in his mind like a burr on a sock.

That week he tested it, in his own quiet way. At school he asked Dan, who attended the church sometimes, whether Christians ever cremated, and Dan shrugged. "My grandpa was. Urn's on the shelf." So it was not a strict rule on either side, more like a strong habit. Victor wrote it out in his notebook like a math problem, drawing a little chart: Hindus, mostly fire, except children and holy people; Christians, mostly earth, but sometimes fire. He tried to work out the ratio of funerals he had actually seen, two burials and one cremation, and gave up, because three was too small a number to mean anything.

In class on Friday, the teacher asked what people believed happened after death, and a boy near the window tried to dismiss the whole question with a joke about ghosts. Victor raised his hand instead and described both funerals, the marigolds and the coffin, the five elements and the clouds, without saying which one he thought was true. Giuseppe, who sat behind him, leaned forward and whispered, "So which is it?" Victor looked down at his notebook, where his chart ended in a blank space he had left on purpose.

"I don't know yet," he said. "Ask me in fifty years."

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: A bond held until its maturity date pays back its full face value, as long as the issuer does not default, no matter how its price moved in between.
story:
Grandpa's porch was the most tranquil spot on the whole street, but Levi couldn't sit still. He had a presentation on Friday about which was riskier, a stock or a bond, and right now his best answer was "um." Joseph had already claimed stocks were riskier, and Joseph had a way of sounding right even when he wasn't, so Levi needed something better than that.

"Grandpa, do you own any stocks?" Levi asked, spinning his pencil on the wobbly table.

"One or two. And a bond." Grandpa shuffled inside and came back with a folder thick with old papers. He set it down, poured his coffee, and left Levi alone with it, which felt like being handed a treasure map with half the markings missing.

Levi found the bond page first. He read it twice. The price line made his stomach drop: the bond was worth less than Grandpa had paid for it, quite a lot less, and it had dipped that way months ago and never fully climbed back. He imagined telling Joseph that bonds were safe, and Joseph laughing and pulling out this exact kind of paper. Levi texted his friend Dexter right there: "Grandpa's bond LOST money. I might have to revise my whole presentation." Dexter replied with a single wide-eyed emoji, which was not helpful.

Then Levi noticed a column he'd skipped, the way you skip the quiet kid in class. It said the bond matured in a few years. He didn't know what that meant at first, so he flipped through the folder like a carnivore hunting through tall grass, page by page, until he found a sheet from when Grandpa bought the thing. Face value, it said, and the number matched exactly what Grandpa would get back at that maturity date. The price had dropped, the price had stayed low, and none of it changed that final number. As long as the company that issued the bond didn't default, Grandpa got the full face value back if he just held on.

"Grandpa," Levi called toward the kitchen, "the price on your bond fell and you didn't sell?"

"Held it. Didn't even watch it that close." Grandpa came back drying his hands. "You checking up on my money now?"

Levi grinned. "Just checking up on my presentation." He spread both pages side by side on the table. The stock page was a jagged line, real gains, real losses, no promised anything at the end. The bond page had a promise printed right on it, steady as a fence post.

On Friday, Levi stood up after Joseph finished. "Joseph says stocks are riskier," Levi said, "and here's why he's right." A few kids laughed. "But watch this." He held up his hand-drawn chart of Grandpa's bond, the scary dip circled in red, the maturity payoff circled in green. "This bond's price fell and stayed down. If Grandpa panicked and sold, he'd lose money, just like a stock. If he holds it until it matures, and the issuer doesn't default, he gets the full face value back no matter what the price did in between." He tapped the red circle. "The risk with a bond isn't the wiggling price line. It's you, selling too early, or the company going under."

Mr. Sánchez, who had wandered in to borrow the projector, stopped in the doorway and raised his eyebrows at Levi. "Did you come up with that yourself?"

Levi looked at Grandpa's chart one more time, then back at the class. "I had good sources."

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: HTML has six levels of headings, h1 to h6, with h1 the most important.
story:
The gym smelled like burnt motors and popcorn, and Ruby had exactly forty minutes before the judges came by the robotics table. Her robot, Django, could stack blocks fine. The problem was the team display, a laptop showing nothing but a blank white page, because their old display file had been deleted when the library computer crashed.

"We need a web page," said Issac, balancing Django's spare arm on his head like a hat. "Ms. Marino said the judges score presentation too."

Ruby opened a text editor and typed the page title between two tags. In robotics club last month, Ms. Marino had written a giant heading on the whiteboard and told them that HTML has six levels of headings, h1 to h6, with h1 the most important. Ruby remembered it because Issac had asked if there was an h7, and Ms. Marino had said the world wasn't ready. Ruby had typed her title as h3, since three felt like a lucky number.

When she loaded the page, the title came out small, like a whisper at a rock concert. "That's the saddest headline I've ever seen," said Louis-Felix, who had come over with a strip of foam insulation tucked under one arm for Django's claw grip. "It's proportional to our chances of winning, actually. Tiny."

"Thanks. Very helpful." Ruby frowned at the screen. The words were there, so the problem wasn't the text. Something invisible was going on, some rule she couldn't see. She thought of the whiteboard again: h1 the most important. Important things get big, probably. She changed the 3 to a 1 and reloaded. The title sprang up big and bold, and Issac cheered so loudly that the team at the next table looked over.

"Can you make it not off to the left like that?" Louis-Felix asked. "It looks like it's hiding from the judges."

Ruby added a style with text-align centered, reloaded, and the heading floated right to the middle of the page. She was so pleased she decided the snack run could be postponed until the page had a photo of Django on it. She hunted through folders while Issac narrated like a sports announcer. "She's going for the picture, folks, she's dragging it in, and it is enormous."

The photo covered the whole screen, ninety percent robot, ten percent chaos. Louis-Felix snorted. "Now that," he said, "is h1 energy."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: During the pubertal growth spurt, hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms, legs and body catch up.
story:
Eve sat on her bedroom floor with both shoes off, staring at her toes. This morning, at the shoe store, the cashier had brought her a size six instead of the five and a half she'd asked for, because the smaller pair pinched. Five and a half had fit fine in September. Now it was barely November, and here she was again, and the worst part was that her jeans still fit perfectly. She dug through her closet to excavate the shoebox from last spring, checked the size printed on the end, and frowned. Two sizes in a year and a half. Something had to be wrong with her, or at least strange.

She taped a strip of paper to her wall and started a chart, because a chart felt more coherent than worrying. She traced her right hand, measured her foot with a ruler, then measured her sleeve length and her inseam, the same way her science teacher, Ms. Leung, had shown them for the plant unit. If her whole body were growing at once, everything should creep up together. But the numbers didn't. Feet, way up since summer. Hands, up. Sleeves, the same. Inseam, the same. She stood back and squinted at the chart like it was a puzzle with one piece hiding underneath the picture.

Her phone buzzed. It was a text from Trenton: "Guess what. My mom made me get new sneakers TODAY. That's the second time this school year. Second! And my jeans still fit fine. Am I turning into some kind of clown-footed mutant? Also did you finish the lab sheet? It's due first period, in case you forgot, which you did."

Eve laughed out loud, alone in her room, and typed back fast. "Not a mutant. Same thing happened to me today, literally today. I made a chart. Hands and feet grow first, before the arms and legs and the rest of the body catch up." She hit send before she could second-guess it. Then she added, "The lab sheet is in my binder, half done. Ms. Leung wants it by first period or it's a zero. I'll finish it in ten minutes if you check my conclusion paragraph."

She flipped open her binder, and the lab sheet was, as promised, half finished, her handwriting slanting downhill the way it did when she was tired. Her pencil moved like a laser, straight down the page, filling in the data table she'd copied from the board. When she got to the conclusion, she paused. The plant data showed the same kind of lag she'd seen on her wall chart, one part shooting ahead while the rest waited its turn. She wrote two careful sentences about that, then photographed the sheet and sent it to Trenton for checking.

He replied with a thumbs up and then, a minute later: "Wait. So my feet are just early? Like they know something the rest of me doesn't yet?" Eve looked from her phone to the paper chart on her wall, at the two big traced feet surrounded by all those unchanged measurements. "Basically," she typed. "The rest of you just has to catch up." She set the phone down, wiggled her toes in their new socks, and drew a small arrow on the chart pointing at the empty space where next month's measurements would go.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A control group is treated exactly like the test group except for the one thing being tested, so any difference can be traced to that change.
story:
Keira crouched between the rows of pea plants in Mr. Hu's garden with her notebook open on her knee. Every plant had been sprayed with the fish fertilizer she had mixed herself, and every plant had grown taller in two weeks. "My hypothesis says the fertilizer makes peas grow faster," she told Kale, who was measuring the tallest vine with a ruler. "And look. Eleven centimeters more than when we started."

Kale wrote the number down, then squinted at the empty bed beside them. "So what did the plants without fertilizer do?" Keira opened her mouth and then closed it. She had not planted any without. Every seed in her tray had gotten the spray, the same water, the same spot of sun, because that had seemed fair. Now she had eleven numbers that added up to nothing she could compare them with. She flipped back through her pages, hunting for something she could cite, some record of untreated peas, but there was only her own handwriting saying, sprayed all of them again.

She found Mr. Hu by the compost bins and told him the problem straight. "I can't tell if the fertilizer worked, because I have nothing to show what the peas would have done anyway." Mr. Hu rubbed dirt off his hands and pointed at the second bed, the one she had walked past every day. "That's why a control group exists," he said. "Treated exactly like the test group except for the one thing being tested, so any difference can be traced to that change." Keira looked at the bed, where Mr. Hu's own peas stood in the same soil, watered on the same schedule, and untouched by anything from her spray bottle.

She measured his plants that afternoon with Kale holding the ruler, and the numbers came out taller. His vines had gained fourteen centimeters while hers had gained eleven. Keira stared at the two columns in her notebook. Her fertilizer had not helped. If anything, the peas without it had grown more, though she was not ready to say why and did not need to.

The next morning she gave her plants a careful inspection, checking undersides of leaves the way her mother checked her rash once and came back with a diagnosis of poison ivy, not bug bites. Along the stems of the fertilized peas she found the edges gone crisp and brown, an abrupt line where green stopped and dry began. She copied the observation down, then capped her spray bottle and set it on the fence post. "Kale," she called across the garden, "get me some seeds. We're starting over, and this time half of everything gets nothing but water."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: A crescendo means gradually getting louder, and a diminuendo or decrescendo means gradually getting softer.
story:
Charlotte had six days to learn "Moonrise March" before the recital on Saturday, and the last page was ruining her. She could play every note with her eyes closed, but the piece sounded flat, like a robot reading a recipe out loud. Her mom had even tucked a blanket under the piano legs to insulate the neighbors from the noise, which meant she could practice as long as she wanted, and she still could not make the music sound like music.

She called Maverick, who was learning the same piece for the same recital. "Play me the last page," she said, holding her phone toward the piano. He played, and she heard the same problem in his version too. They both slammed straight into the loud parts like a door swinging open in the wind, then dropped to quiet just as suddenly.

"It's that little sideways triangle thing," Maverick said. "Ms. Addo wrote crescendo under mine in red pen, and there's another word, diminuendo, right after."

"A crescendo means gradually getting louder," Charlotte said slowly, reading from her own copy of the sheet. "Not all at once. Gradually. And the other word must be the opposite, getting softer bit by bit." She looked at the hairs on her arm. "That's why it sounded wrong. We've been stepping straight off a cliff instead of walking down the stairs."

She tested it with sticky notes. Above each measure with the crescendo she wrote "1, 2, 3," meaning soft, medium, loud, one step per bar. Then she played, watching the numbers like a staircase. The sound built the way a wave rolls in toward the shore instead of splashing down like a bucket of water. For the diminuendo she reversed the numbers, and the ending faded until the last note was barely a breath.

"You have to be consistent," she told Maverick when she called him back. "Same amount louder each bar. If you skip a step, it's the cliff all over again." He tried it while she listened, and she heard him climbing evenly this time, then easing back down. "Better," she said. "Do it five times tonight."

After he hung up, she played the whole last page once more, from the hairpin triangle to the final low C. Sunlight lay across the carpet near the window, and a mushroom she'd noticed on the lawn that morning, a squat brown decomposer doing its slow quiet work on a fallen branch, sat just visible at the edge of the glass. She played the crescendo one step at a time, then let the sound shrink away to nothing.

"Gradually," she said, and turned the page.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population.
story:
The after-school geography club met in the library on Tuesdays, at the table by the window where the afternoon light caught the green lichen on the old stone sill outside. Sawyer spread his project across the table: a bar graph of the ethnic and cultural origins of a small town in Manitoba, drawn from census numbers he had copied onto a fresh sheet. Ryland leaned over it, chewing the end of a pencil.

"Your graph is broken," Ryland said. "The bars add up to a hundred and forty percent."

Sawyer checked his arithmetic twice. He had not made a mistake. Scottish, ten percent. Ukrainian, eight. Filipino, six. Ojibwe, four. On and on it went, past a hundred and climbing, which was impossible, or at least it looked impossible. He wanted the graph finished by Friday for the club display, and a graph that lied was worse than no graph. Darwin, who had joined the club mostly to draw maps but stayed for the arguments, suggested that people in the town simply counted wrong.

"People don't count their own grandmothers wrong," Sawyer said. He sat back and looked at the bars again. Then he tried something. He drew a circle around his own family in his notebook. His mother's side was Scottish and Cree. His father's side was Ukrainian. If a form asked him where his people came from, he would not pick one. He would write all three. He drew three small tally marks beside his own name.

"Oh," he said. "People can put down more than one."

He searched the census website on the library computer and found the sentence he needed. Since 1981, it said, the Canadian census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population. He read it aloud, and Ryland frowned, then laughed.

"So the graph isn't wrong. The town is just full of people like you."

"Like everybody," Sawyer said. He remembered the club's heritage week in the fall, when Mr. Nielsen, who ran the club, had taped a long paper banner to the wall and asked everyone to write where their families came from. Half the students had written two or three things. Darwin had written four and run out of room, which was ironic, since Darwin always said he was the most boring kid in the grade.

Sawyer redrew the graph with a note under the title: totals add up to more than one hundred percent because people may report more than one origin. Then, on the display board, he added the banner idea. Each club member would write their origins on a strip of paper, and the strips would overlap at the corners, the way the numbers did.

On Friday, Mr. Nielsen read the note and nodded slowly. "Good graph," he said. "Most people never notice that."

Sawyer pinned his own strip to the board: Scottish, Cree, Ukrainian, the letters careful and small. Darwin pinned his four, then mimicked a trumpet fanfare with his mouth, and the whole table burst out laughing.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The thin inner skin of an onion is only one cell thick, so light passes through it and single cells can be seen under a microscope.
story:
Bentley set the old microscope on the picnic table in the backyard and peeled a fat slice of onion off the one his dad had been chopping for dinner. Mr. Rossi had lent him the microscope from his garage, and tomorrow the whole class had to hand in a labeled drawing of onion cells. Keith leaned over his shoulder, holding his phone sideways to document the whole experiment for the group project, because his teacher had promised bonus points for video evidence. "You are about to witness science," Keith announced, in his best documentary voice, which sounded like a sleepy news anchor.

Bentley dropped the thick onion slice onto the slide, clamped it under the clips, and peered into the eyepiece. He saw nothing. Not blurred nothing, but black nothing, as if someone had put a lid over the sun. "The bulb burned out," Keith guessed. Bentley shook his head and tried the lamp on the stage; it shone brightly and the view stayed black. "It's the onion," he said slowly. "The light can't get through it."

He sat back and remembered a rainy afternoon last spring, when Aria had pressed a maple leaf against the classroom window and complained that she couldn't see any of the veins because it was too thick. She had held up a piece of onion skin instead, thin as fog, and joked that you could probably read a newspaper through it. Bentley stared at the onion in his hand. Maybe thickness was the whole problem. "Give me your neutral-colored shirt as a background," he told Keith, holding the onion up to the light, "so I can see what I'm doing." Keith held out the pale gray sleeve with great ceremony.

Bentley cut the onion in half and peeled one of the rings apart with tweezers until a papery film came loose from the inside curve. He laid that film on a clean slide, added a drop of water, and lowered the cover slip. Through the eyepiece, the darkness was gone. Cells appeared like a brick wall built by someone who had been a little tired that day, each one a neat rounded box with a darker dot inside. "Whoa," Keith said, nearly dropping the phone. "You found the bricks."

"Cell wall," Bentley said, drawing the outer edge of each box on his worksheet. "Membrane, just inside it. And that dot is the nucleus." He marked all three, then slid over so Keith could look while the phone recorded over his shoulder. "So the thin inner skin is only one cell thick," Bentley said, grinning, "and that's why light passes through it." Keith filmed the slide, the worksheet, and then, for no reason anyone could defend, his own elbow. "That's for the credits," he said.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The bandwagon technique urges people to do or buy something because "everyone else is," appealing to the wish to belong rather than giving a reason.
story:
Parker had forty dollars and one goal: new sneakers before Saturday's tryouts, because his old ones had a hole where the toe seam used to be. He found the pair he wanted in the mall's shoe store window, and above them a screen flashed the words JOIN THE MILLIONS WHO ALREADY SWITCHED. He stared at it, then at the shoes. Millions? His whole school didn't have a million people in it.

Caroline and Archie caught up with him inside the store, where a wall of screens cycled through ads. A famous soccer player's face filled the biggest one, saying these shoes made him unstoppable. "He's paid to say that," Caroline said, arms crossed. "It's a celebrity testimonial. My sister fell for one with a phone case that cracked in a week."

"The millions thing is bugging me more," Parker said. He picked up the display shoe and turned it over. "Everyone else is buying them. So what? Everyone else is a reason to feel left out, not a reason the shoe is good." Archie snorted. "It's called a bandwagon appeal. We just did it in Mr. Pérez's class last week. You were drawing a propeller on your notebook." Parker remembered the propeller, at least. He had not remembered the lesson.

They wandered the mall to think, and Parker kept noticing the pattern everywhere: a smoothie stand claimed "the drink everyone's talking about," a phone kiosk bragged about "the millions who switched." Nobody said what the product actually did better. It was like the ads were biased toward making him feel like the odd one out, so he would pay to rejoin the crowd. He tested the idea on Archie. "Quick, what does the sneaker ad say the shoe does better?" Archie opened his mouth, closed it, and shrugged. "Nothing. It just says millions." Exactly, Parker thought, and steered them back toward the shoe store.

At the counter he tried to negotiate. "Display pair, half price?" The cashier shook her head, but pointed at a rack behind him: last year's model, same sole, different color, thirty percent off. Parker compared them sole to sole, bent both heels, checked the stitching. The old ones felt the same. The new ones just had a bigger ad budget.

He walked out with the older model and eleven dollars still in his pocket. Archie clapped him on the shoulder. "Tryouts Saturday?" "Tryouts Saturday," Parker said, and stopped to retie the laces of a shoe nobody's ad had ever mentioned.

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: The minor pentatonic scale has five notes; in A, they are A, C, D, E and G, and many blues solos are built from it.
story:
Grandpa's turntable was spinning a record with more scratches than music, so Carter had claimed the corner armchair, his borrowed guitar flat across his knees. The problem was simple and enormous: tomorrow he had to improvise a blues solo in music class, and so far his fingers only knew how to play the same four notes in the same tired order.

"I don't get how you make something up on the spot," Bethany said from the rug, where she was building a house out of playing cards. "It's like being asked to tell a joke on demand."

"It's worse," Carter said. "It's like being told the joke has to rhyme, be funny, and last exactly twelve bars."

Blaire, who had brought her harmonica mostly as an accessory, blew a single flat note that made the dog leave the room. "Maybe the trick is that you're not actually making it all up," she said. "Grandpa said something about that."

Grandpa was found in the kitchen, arguing with a crossword. Carter asked him how a solo could be both made up and not made up, and Grandpa tapped his pen against the table. "Minor pentatonic," he said. "Five notes. In A, that's A, C, D, E and G. Most blues solos are built out of those." Then he went back to seven down, a word for prehistoric, nine letters, and Carter let him have his extinct mammoths in peace.

Five notes. Carter sat back down and worked it out like a math problem. If any of the five notes would fit over the chords, then he wasn't inventing a language from nothing, he was just rearranging words he already had. That was a different thing entirely. He tested the idea right there: Bethany strummed the progression off a video on her phone, the twelve bars going around like a conveyor belt, and Carter picked his five notes one at a time. Some landed gracefully. One, the C, landed like a dropped plate, but even the dropped plate sounded, weirdly, bluesy.

"Again," he said, and Bethany complied, and this time he left space between the notes instead of cramming them in like a suitcase. The space helped. He leaned into the G, bent it slightly, and Blaire said "oh" in a surprised voice, which from Blaire was practically a standing ovation.

They went around the progression four more times. On the fifth, Carter stopped watching his fingers and just listened to where his hand wanted to go next, like the notes were arguing and he was the jury deciding which one got to speak. His mouth was doing something he hadn't authorized. It was smiling.

"One more time," he said, "and then I'll do the slow one, the sad one."

Bethany hit play on the phone.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
story:
Natalie spread her crumpled data table across the library table and weighted the corners with books about volcanoes. Her project tested whether music made plants grow faster, and she had measured bean sprouts every day for three weeks. The numbers looked good. The graph did not. It looked like a random scribble.

"You put the days on the wrong side," said Mahmoud, sliding into the chair across from her. He was building a ramp-and-marble project two tables over, and he had wandered over twice already, supposedly to borrow a pencil.

"The days are right here," Natalie said, tapping the vertical edge of her graph. "See, one, seven, fourteen. And the sprout heights go along the bottom."

Mahmoud tilted his head. "That's backwards. The thing you change goes across, the thing that happens goes up." He tapped the horizontal axis. "Days across. Heights up. Everybody does it that way."

"Everybody is not a reason."

"Ms. Nair marked me down for it last year," he said. "She wrote a whole paragraph."

Natalie frowned at her graph. The days were what she controlled; time passed at the same rate no matter what she did, and the heights were what came out of it. If she wanted anyone to see whether the music sprouts accelerated past the silent ones after day ten, the pattern had to run left to right, the way eyes travel. She pulled a fresh sheet toward her.

At the next table, Alexandra looked up from her laptop. "If you're redrawing, leave room for a title. Mine's called 'The Mystery of the Muddy Water,' and I haven't even solved it yet."

"I solved mine," Natalie said. "Probably."

She drew the new axes, days along the bottom, heights up the side, and plotted her points one by one. Halfway through she stopped. The music sprouts were ahead, but only the ones by the window speaker. The library speaker, the one in the quiet corner, had done nothing at all, or close to nothing. On her old graph the two groups had looked the same because the layout was a negligent mess that buried the difference. On the new one it jumped out.

"Mahmoud. Come look at this."

He leaned over. "The window ones won."

"It's not the music," Natalie said slowly. "It's the window. More light. The music group was just sitting in the better spot the whole time."

"That's a twist," said Alexandra, who had drifted over to see.

Natalie flipped to a blank page and wrote a new title at the top: "Does My Experiment Prove Anything?" Then, underneath it, "Part Two: The Window." She started sketching a plan with equal light on both sides, twelve new beans, and a shelf in her garage.

Mahmoud pointed at her fresh sheet. "Days still go across, right?"

"Days go across," Natalie said, and drew the first axis.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: A boundary is a limit a person sets about what they are comfortable with, such as how others treat them, touch them or use their belongings.
story:
Easton sat on the edge of his bed with his laptop open, but he wasn't typing. Kyan had gone quiet in their video game chat three days ago, and tonight Kyan's little brother had texted: he won't come out of his room. Easton stared at the chat window and tried to quantify the problem, to count the days Kyan had seemed off, but the numbers kept sliding around. Seven short answers. Two ignored invites. One cancelled sleepover. Something was wrong, and he couldn't see it directly.

He picked up his phone and called Dan, who answered on the second ring, chewing something.

"I think it's us," Dan said. "I read his messages on his phone last week. He left it on the lunch table, and I just picked it up and started reading. He saw me do it and grabbed it back, and now he barely talks."

Easton looked across his room at the model rocket on his shelf, half painted, its nose cone still grey. "Did you ask before you read it?"

"Why would I ask? We're friends."

Easton didn't have an answer right away. The radiator ticked under the window, and outside a car door slammed somewhere down the street. "Kyan's brother says he's not coming out of his room. That could be stress, or anxiety, or something else. But he got quiet right after the phone thing."

"So what do we do, apologize?"

Easton tested the idea out loud. "A boundary is a limit someone sets about what they're comfortable with, like how you treat them or use their stuff. His phone is his stuff. We crossed it." Dan was quiet for a second, and Easton could hear him stop chewing.

"That actually makes sense," Dan said. "Okay. Apology first."

On Saturday, Easton and Dan stood outside Kyan's door, which felt like the last frontier of a long journey, though it was only one hallway. Dan knocked. "It's us. Five minutes. Then we leave you alone if you want."

The door opened a crack. Kyan looked tired, hair flat on one side. "I'm not mad anymore," he said. "I was just..." He shrugged. "Everything felt loud. My mom says it was stress. I'm working on coping. She got me this breathing thing. It's kind of dumb but it helps."

"It wasn't dumb of you to want your phone left alone," Easton said. "That's your boundary. Next time we ask before touching it."

Kyan opened the door wider. "You two are obstinate, you know that? Camping outside my room like geese." But he was almost smiling.

Dan held up a bag from the corner store. "Chips. And we brought the new map download."

Kyan looked at the bag, then at the two of them, and stepped back to let them in. "Xbox's already on."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: A eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died; the word comes from Greek roots meaning to 'speak well of'.
story:
Jacob's mother handed him a folded card at the door of Grandma Ruth's house, where the whole family had gathered after the funeral. "You're saying something tomorrow, remember. Just a few words." He had said yes to this three weeks ago, when Grandma was still awake enough to squeeze his hand, and now that the moment had arrived he could not remember why he had agreed. A speech, in front of everybody, about a person who could not hear it.

He found the card table in the back room, where his cousins had set up a puzzle, and sat down with a notebook. Paxton from next door had come along because his own parents were away, and he slid into the chair across from Jacob. "What are you writing?"

"The thing for tomorrow. My mom says it's called a eulogy." Jacob frowned at the word. "I don't actually know what that means, exactly."

"Look it up," Paxton said, and nodded toward the dictionary on Grandma's shelf, the fat red one with the cracked spine that always fell open to the same page because Grandma had pressed flowers in it. Jacob carried it to the table, and the flowers slid out, dry and brown. He found the entry. "A speech praising a person who has died," he read quietly. It said the word came from Greek roots meaning "speak well of." So the whole job was to speak well of her. That helped a little, and it also made the problem sharper, because he had to choose what to praise, and he had exactly one memory that felt true enough.

Loralie, his cousin, leaned over from the puzzle. "Just say she was nice. Everyone says that."

"She was nice," Jacob said, "but if I say that, nobody will learn anything they didn't already know." He turned the flower over in his fingers. The problem, as he saw it, was that a eulogy had to show her, not just tell about her, the way a good chapter shows a character doing something instead of the author saying he was brave. So he needed the right scene. He tested memories the way he tested guesses in science class. The summer she taught him to fix the porch swing, but he had quit halfway and she finished it alone. The time she let him fail at bread so he would understand dough. He crossed both out.

Then he remembered the winter her eyesight began to deteriorate, and how she kept reading anyway, running her finger under each line and asking him to turn the pages when her hand got tired. He had never once been asked to do it; it was voluntary, something he chose every visit because she never made him feel he had to. That was the memory. That showed the kind of person she was without saying it.

The next morning, the folding chairs were set up in the backyard under the big maple, and when his turn came, Mr. Pham, her oldest neighbor, gave his elbow a small pat as he passed. Jacob stood at the front with the flower pressed flat inside his notebook. He told about the reading, the finger under the line, the turning pages nobody asked him to turn. When he finished, Loralie was crying, and his mother was crying, and Mr. Pham was nodding like Jacob had proven something.

Afterward Paxton caught him by the drinks table. "You spoke well of her," he said.

"That's literally what the word means," Jacob said, and for the first time in three weeks, he smiled.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: In Spanish, the masculine plural "hermanos" can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together, so "Tengo dos hermanos" might describe one brother and one sister.
story:
Ms. Almeida had taped a sign to the classroom door that said Bienvenidos, which Grace had taken as a personal challenge, since the class was now three weeks old and she still mixed up gato and gata whenever she got nervous. Today's assignment was on the board: describe your family and pets in full sentences. No single words. No pointing at photographs and hoping.

Grace had prepared. She had a mother, a father, a little brother named Sam, a goldfish named Dwight, and a grandmother who lived in the apartment upstairs and belonged, Grace had decided, in every sentence about the family anyway. She wrote Tengo un hermano at the top of her page and underlined it twice, which was the kind of thing that looked like confidence but cost nothing.

Across the room, Julia stood up to read hers. Julia was the sort of person who volunteered first and apologized later. "Tengo dos hermanos," she said, clear as a bell, and then sat down looking pleased with herself.

Joey's hand shot up so fast his chair squeaked. "That's wrong," he said. "Julia, I've been to your house. You have a brother and a sister. Hermanos is brothers. You said you have two brothers, which is a lie in two languages."

"Take it up with the textbook," Julia said, and flipped it around so the whole class could see the page she'd copied from, because arguing with Julia was a full-contact sport and she liked to bring equipment.

Grace looked from Julia to the textbook to her own page, where un hermano sat underlined and suddenly suspicious. She remembered Julia's actual family: one brother, one sister. She remembered the sentence. Then she thought about her own sentence, Tengo un hermano, and realized the plural must work like a big bin that held both kinds. If Julia with a mixed pair could say dos hermanos, then hermanos couldn't mean only brothers, or at least couldn't have to. It could cover the whole group, whichever mix was in it. Grace tested the idea against everything she'd heard that week: Ms. Almeida saying mis padres for a mother and a father, the word abuelos that seemed to stretch over both grandmothers and grandfathers. The pattern held. The masculine plural was the one doing double duty, and Julia had just let it.

"Okay," Grace said out loud, before she could decide not to. "Hermanos means brothers, or brothers and sisters together. So Tengo dos hermanos could be one of each. Julia's sentence is fine."

Ms. Almeida raised one eyebrow, which was her version of applause. "The jury has reached a verdict," she said, and Grace felt the word land somewhere in her chest like a small trophy.

"That's so aggressive," Joey muttered, but he crossed out his correction, which was the closest thing to an apology he had in him. Grace slid her pencil down to the bottom of her page and wrote a new sentence, slowly, the way you do when you want every letter to behave: Tengo un hermano y una hermana. O dos hermanos. Either way, Sam was going to hate sharing.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing guitar strings repeatedly makes the fingertips sore at first; with regular practice, the skin toughens into calluses and playing hurts less.
story:
Abigail set her guitar case on the bench and did not open it. Ms. Zhang's studio was a converted garage with sparse furniture, just two stools, a rug, and a wall of sheet music, and Abigail had decided she was done with all of it.

"You're quiet today," Ms. Zhang said, tuning a student guitar.

"My fingers hurt." Abigail held out her left hand. The tips of her first three fingers were red and dented, each one marked with a thin line across it. "Every time I press the strings it stings. I practice, it hurts more. Maybe guitar isn't for me."

Before Ms. Zhang could answer, the door opened and Giuliano came in for his lesson after hers, shaking rain off his jacket. He heard the last part. "I quit for exactly that reason," he said. "One week. My fingers killed and I thought, this instrument is broken or I am."

"You never told me that," Abigail said.

"You never asked why I played recorder instead." He shrugged. "That was two years ago."

Ms. Zhang was writing something in her planner, and Abigail studied her while she waited. Then a thought stopped her cold. It wasn't the guitar. Giuliano had a different guitar and his fingers had hurt too. Abigail's friend Emeric at school played a guitar borrowed from his cousin, and he complained about the same sting. Three guitars, three sets of fingers, one problem. Whatever it was, it came from the pressing itself, not from any particular instrument.

"I want to test something," Abigail said. "Can I try your guitar?" She took the student guitar Ms. Zhang had just tuned, made a chord, and pressed down hard. It stung exactly the same. So it wasn't her strings. It was just what happened when you pressed strings over and over, at least at first. "Then the answer is to practice more, not less," she said slowly, working it out aloud. "Not longer. Just every day, a little."

"That is an idea worth testing," Ms. Zhang said, and did not say anything else about it, which Abigail later decided was very wise of her.

Two weeks later, Abigail sat on the same bench with her sleeve rolled up, showing Giuliano her fingertips.
