The skin there had grown noticeably thicker, rough little pads where the smooth soreness used to be. "They're calluses," she said. "It barely hurts now. You could still come back, you know. Ms. Zhang said she kept your folder."

Giuliano looked at the wall of sheet music for a long moment. "Half her students quit when the factory closed and the recession hit," he said. "She must get lonely in this garage."

Abigail slid off her stool and opened her guitar case. "Then you'd better warm up," she said, "because your lesson starts in five minutes, and I'm not going anywhere."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869.
story:
The laminated element cards were spread across the lab bench like a game of memory, and Isabella had ninety seconds to find carbon's protons before the bell. The trouble was that the card gave her a number, 6, and the word "carbon," and nothing else. She could not see protons. Nobody could. She would have to trust that the number meant something.

"Time," said Amaya, tapping the wall clock, whose brass mechanism had been ticking through science classes since before their parents were born. "What did you get?"

"Six," Isabella said. "I think."

Chantelle frowned at her own card. "How do you know it's not the number of something else? Electrons, maybe. It's ambiguous. It's just a number sitting there."

Isabella turned her card over, then over again, as if the answer might be hidden on the back. Last spring flashed into her mind, the science museum trip, the hallway where workers were about to renovate the whole west wing and everything smelled like dust and paint. On the timeline wall she had stopped at a glass case. Amaya had tugged her sleeve to keep moving, but Isabella had read the plaque twice: Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869. Below the words was a copy of his chart, and she remembered being surprised at how few elements it held, like a half-finished crossword.

"Ms. Mansour," Isabella called, standing up. "Mendeleev made his table in 1869, right? Before that, how did anybody know what was missing?"

Ms. Mansour smiled but didn't answer, which Isabella took to mean figure it out. She laid out nitrogen, oxygen, and neon in a row, cards side by side. Seven, eight, ten. She covered each atomic number with her thumb and tried to guess it from the element's name alone, then uncovered it. Wrong, wrong, wrong. The number wasn't something you could work out from the name. It had to be counted from inside the atom itself, something you took on trust because the pattern held every single time. That was the test, and the test had passed.

She picked up the carbon card again and held it up so Chantelle could see. "Six protons. That's what the atomic number is. It's not ambiguous at all once you check it."

Chantelle squinted at her own card, then wrote "17 protons" beside chlorine and slid it across the bench. "Prove me wrong."

Isabella grabbed the card and started counting on her fingers.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: If prices rise faster than a savings account's interest rate, the money in the account buys less each year even though the balance grows.
story:
Nicolas spread five years of bank statements across the kitchen table like treasure maps. He had deposited two hundred dollars when he was eight, and every month since, the balance had crept upward. Simple interest, the first statement said, then compound after the bank changed its rules. He grinned at the newest number. Three hundred and twelve dollars, and tomorrow he was finally walking to the bike shop.

Kya came over after dinner, still holding her skateboard. "Let me see," she said, leaning over the papers. She picked up the oldest statement, then the newest, and held them side by side. "Wait. Your money made more once it compounded. The interest started earning its own interest. That part's great."

"It's great," Nicolas said, but he was frowning at his laptop screen. The same bike he had wanted at eight, the red one with the quick-release wheels, was listed on the shop's website. He scrolled and his stomach dropped. Three hundred and ninety dollars.

Parker arrived just then, sniffing around for leftover pizza, and the three of them stared at the screen together. "So your money grew," Parker said slowly, "and the bike grew faster."

"That's it," Nicolas said. He grabbed a pencil and drew two arrows on the back of an envelope, one climbing gently for his account, one climbing more steeply for the price. Through his new lens, the whole five years looked different. Every birthday dollar, every allowance he had skipped lunch to add, all of it had thrived on paper, and it still had not kept up. "The balance goes up every single year," he said, "but prices went up faster, so my money buys less now than it would have back then. It's like running uphill on a hill that's getting steeper."

Ms. Qureshi, who was watering her tomatoes through the open window next door, had been half listening. "The word for that is inflation," she said, and went back to her tomatoes.

The gradual climb on his envelope suddenly seemed like the most important thing Nicolas had ever drawn. He looked at Kya, then at Parker, then at his jar of birthday money on the counter. He poured it out and counted it, coins rolling everywhere.

"Forty-one dollars and change," he announced. "Kya, does the shop still do that used-bike rack in the back?"

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself.
story:
Grace arrived at the cultural festival with a rolled-up poster under her arm and a problem in her head. The poster was for the sign-language club that Kailyn ran at school, and across the top Grace had painted the words "deaf pride" in big blue letters. But that morning Kailyn had grabbed her sleeve in the hallway and said, "One thing's wrong, but I'm not telling you what. You have to figure it out before the festival starts." Then she had disappeared into the crowd, leaving Grace to carry the mystery around all afternoon.

The festival filled the whole park. Safa was working at her family's booth, hanging photographs of terraced fields and explaining to anyone who stopped that the steep green steps in the pictures were ancient agriculture, farmland built right into the mountainside. A man nearby sold bread and told everyone it was his grandmother's recipe. A woman in a bright headwrap taught children a welcome dance from her hometown. Everyone, Grace noticed, had a way of saying who they were and where they came from, and nobody said it the same way twice.

"Maybe it's the colors," Safa suggested, squinting at the poster. "Blue seems subjective to me, but Kailyn loves blue." Grace held the poster up to the light and turned it one way, then another. The paint was even, the letters were straight, the drawings of hands signing looked right because Kailyn herself had checked those. She tried to interpret the poster the way a stranger would, someone walking past a booth at a noisy festival. What would they read first?

She wandered toward the far end of the park, where a small stage hosted performers. A group of dancers wore shirts that said "proud and Deaf" in gold letters, and a woman on stage interpreted the announcements into sign language, her hands moving like quick birds. Grace stood very still. Gold letters. Capital D. She looked at her own poster, at her careful lowercase "deaf," and her stomach did a small flip.

She found Kailyn at the club booth, breathless. "The D. It has to be capital." Kailyn grinned and pointed to a folded paper on the table, a copy of a page from a linguistics book. "In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users," she read aloud, "and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself. Big D is who we are. Little d is just the ear."

Grace borrowed a gold paint pen from the dancer with the quick hands and, while a crowd gathered to watch, turned every small d into a capital D, stroke by careful stroke. "There," she said, holding it up. "Now say it again." Kailyn raised her hands and signed the word, and the whole booth burst into applause.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Airplane mode turns off a phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts.
story:
Brayden's new phone had been his for exactly six hours, and so far it had received one text, from his mom, asking if he had his phone. He was sitting on Jesse's basement couch, holding the phone up like it was a dying firefly. Jesse sat beside him, bouncing a stress ball off the ceiling.

"Three people said they'd text me," Brayden said. "Sonia swore she'd send the group photo. Nothing." The screen showed zero bars where Sonia's phone showed four, sitting right next to his on the armrest. That was the part that bothered him. Same room, same couch, same air.

"Your phone's broken," Jesse said. "Mine did that before I dropped it in the sink." Jesse's own phone was currently in a bag of rice on the kitchen counter, which made him exactly the expert nobody wanted. He wanted, more than anything, to be the one who fixed it, because then the whole afternoon would belong to him.

Brayden turned the phone over. Then he turned it back and swiped down from the top, because Sonia had shown him that trick at school. A row of little buttons appeared, and one of them was a tiny airplane, glowing orange. He inferred that an orange button was probably a button doing something, since the gray ones looked asleep.

"What's airplane mode?" he asked.

"It's for planes," Jesse said, with the confidence of someone who had never been on one.

Brayden pressed it. The orange went gray. In the corner, the zero bars shivered, and then climbed, one, two, three, four. The phone buzzed so hard it nearly slid off the armrest. Then it buzzed again. And again.

He opened the messages. There was the group photo, there was Sonia's review of the school talent show, and there was a long debate about whether the class should vote on the field trip or just let Ms. Farah pick, Sonia arguing that even a bus destination deserved democracy. All of it had arrived while his phone sat silent in his pocket, holding every message like a mailbox with no mail carrier.

"So airplane mode turns off the signals," Brayden said. "The cellular connection. Calls, texts, all of it." It had to have been on since the store, when the cashier had tapped around on the screen before handing it over. His phone hadn't been broken. It had been quiet on purpose, like a demure two hundred dollar brick. The basement, which had felt a bit desolate during the hour of silence, now seemed louder, busier, better.

"Technically I fixed it," Jesse said. "I said press a button."

"You said it was broken."

"Broken buttons get pressed. That's how fixing works."

Brayden typed to Sonia: got my phone working. send everything again. Then he tipped sideways into the couch cushion and read the whole talent show argument twice.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
story:
Matteo sat on the edge of his bed with the trumpet in his lap, glaring at the dented case on the floor. His lesson with Ms. Bautista was tomorrow, and once again he had waited until Sunday to practice. He played the warm-up scale, and his fingers stumbled at the same spot they always stumbled, the tricky jump in the third bar of "Sunny Valley Suite."

Issa knocked on his open door, holding her flute case like a lunchbox. "Are you ready for the duet? I want us to try out together next month, and Ms. Bautista picks people who sound prepared." She flopped onto the rug. "You've been playing that same bar for ten minutes."

"It keeps falling apart," Matteo said. He played it again, and again his fingers missed. He stared at the music, then at the calendar above his desk, where he'd written LESSON in red pen every Monday for the past month. Something nagged at him. He had practiced plenty of time, maybe two whole hours last Sunday, and yet Monday's lesson had gone badly anyway. He'd been assuming the problem was the bar itself, that it was just hard. But Issa played harder passages than that, and hers sounded agile and easy.

"When do you practice?" he asked her.

"After school, like twenty minutes, mostly every day," she said. "Why?"

Matteo flipped the calendar pages backward. Four red Mondays, four long Sunday evenings, four bad lessons. He had crammed all his time into one session right before each lesson, and the mistakes never left. He thought about his father's garden, how seeds watered a little each day came up stronger than a bucket dumped on them once. Maybe his fingers worked the same way.

"New plan," he said. "I'm going to split it up. Short practice, every day, not one big panic on Sundays."

"For how long?" Issa asked.

"Same total time. Just spread out over the days." He picked the trumpet back up and played the third bar once, slowly, then set it down. "Starting tomorrow, right after school. You knock on my door on your way home."

For the rest of the evening he left the trumpet in its case. On Monday he played the bar for Ms. Bautista, and it still wobbled. But by Thursday, after four short sessions, his fingers found the notes without his having to think, and he could finally distinguish the melody's echo phrase from its opening one, something he'd never managed before.

Issa stood in the doorway listening, tapping her foot. "Same time tomorrow?"

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Chicago's Engine Company 21 is widely credited with the first fire pole, installed in 1878 after a firefighter slid down a pole faster than others could take the stairs.
story:
The hay ride had been fun for about ten minutes, until the wheels sank into a muddy rut and everyone had to climb off and push. Ellie stood in the drizzle with Mohamed-Amine and Dash, boots sinking too, while Mr. Reyes, the farmer who owned the place, waved them toward the big red barn. "Might as well look inside while we wait for the tractor to be pulled out," he said. "There's something in there you don't usually see on a farm."

The barn smelled like hay and old paint. In the center of the main floor, between stalls that now held saddles and feed buckets, a polished brass pole ran from a hole in the loft floor all the way down to a rubber mat beside them. Dash grabbed it immediately and shinned halfway up like a monkey, until the teacher called him down.

"Why would a barn have a pole?" Dash asked. "Lofts have ladders. Or stairs." He pointed to the steep wooden staircase in the corner, which was cluttered with crates marked as cargo for the farm store, canned tomatoes and jars of honey.

"That's the question, all right," Mr. Reyes said, but he didn't say anything else. He just smiled and went back out to the mud to deal with the tractor, which seemed to Ellie like a hint. He wanted them to figure it out.

Mohamed-Amine climbed the stairs first, counting under his breath, then stomped down again, careful not to knock over the cargo. "Fourteen seconds," he reported. "And I nearly broke my ankle."

"Nobody slides down a pole by accident on purpose," Dash said. "There has to be a reason."

Ellie looked up at the hole in the loft floor, then at the rubber mat, which was worn pale in the middle. A mat doesn't wear out from ladders, she thought. It wears out from feet landing on it, over and over, fast. And the pole was brass, polished bright, not rusty like the hinges and the nail heads everywhere else in this barn. Somebody had kept it shiny for a long time.

"Time me," she said, and climbed the stairs. At the top, she wrapped her legs and arms around the pole, took a breath, and let go. The slide was faster than she expected, and she landed on the mat with a thump that shook the honey jars. Mohamed-Amine stared at the stopwatch on his phone. "Five seconds. Nine seconds faster."

"So the pole exists because it's faster," Dash said. "That's kind of trivial, isn't it? Everything fast exists because it's faster."

"It's not trivial if seconds matter," Ellie said. "What happens in a barn where seconds matter?" She looked around slowly. Wide doors, tall enough for a wagon. Hooks on the ceiling, empty now. The red paint, brighter than barn paint usually was. "I don't think this was ever a barn," she said. "I think it was a fire station."

Mohamed-Amine had wandered to a trunk in the corner, half hidden under a tarp, and lifted the lid. Inside were folded canvas buckets and a brittle newspaper clipping. He held it up to the light from the door, and Ellie read over his shoulder. It was about Chicago's Engine Company 21, and a pole installed there in 1878, after one firefighter slid down a pole faster than the others could take the stairs.

"First fire pole ever," Ellie read out loud. "Right here, well, not here, but this exact thing."

When Mr. Reyes came back in, muddy to the knees, she told him what she'd figured out, and he laughed. "My grandfather salvaged the whole building when the city tore the station down. Best thing he ever hauled home." He looked at the pole. "Want another slide before the tractor's ready?"

Ellie was already at the top of the stairs.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: According to the U.S. Fire Administration, failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect.
story:
Sofia had forty minutes before her grandmother's laundry had to be out of the machine, because the whole family was arriving at noon for Tía Rosa's birthday lunch, and every chair needed the good tablecloth. Abuela had gone to the bakery, so the laundry was Sofia's job, and she was determined to do it right. She remembered being nine, standing on a stool in this same basement, watching Abuela separate a mountain of clothes into piles like a card dealer. Whites here, darks there, towels separate because they generated lint that clung to everything else. Sofia had thought it looked easy. It was not.

She sorted on the cold concrete floor: a dark pile of jeans and a navy tablecloth, a pale pile of shirts, a middle pile she squinted at suspiciously. One pink sock had snuck into the whites. She fished it out, remembering a ruined load from years ago when a red bandana turned a whole basket of undershirts pink. Not this time. She measured the detergent, stuffed the tablecloth and the darks into the washer, and started it before ten thirty.

The washer's spin cycle thundered like a train, and the basement smelled of detergent and damp stone. While she waited, she heard a thumping from the corner. The dryer was running, though nothing was in the washer except her load. She yanked the dryer door open. Inside was a single wet towel going around and around, and behind it, in the slot at the door's edge, a mat of lint so thick and grey it looked like felt. She peeled it out in one piece, and it was shockingly heavy, like a small dead animal.

Sofia stared at it. The dryer had felt hot when she opened it, hotter than it should for one towel. She remembered something Mr. Tang, the neighbour who had been a firefighter, said at the block party last summer, standing by the grill with a paper plate: "Failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires. Lint builds up, blocks the airflow, and heat collects." He had said the U.S. Fire Administration tracked it. Sofia had nodded politely then. Now the grey mat sat in her hand like evidence.

She felt around the slot for more lint and pulled out a second clump. Then she had an idea she could test. If the airflow was blocked, the dryer should take too long to dry things. She fished the towel out, wrung it, and draped it over a chair to air dry instead. She would time her own load once the washer finished, and if it still ran long with a clean filter, she would tell Abuela the problem was deeper in the machine. Until then, the lint was not going back in. Lint was supposed to be the dryer's adversary, but here it had been living rent-free for what looked like months.

Upstairs, feet pounded, and Mariah appeared in the doorway with a birthday gift bag, early as always. "Your grandma let me in. Are you hiding down here?"

"Look at this," Sofia said, holding up the lint mat. "Nobody's been cleaning the filter. Mr. Tang said this is the number one reason dryers catch fire. Lint blocks the airflow and heat builds up." Mariah's eyes went wide, and she poked the mat with one finger.

"That's been in there the whole time? That's so negligent."

"I know. Abuela can't see the slot anymore, I think." The washer beeped its final beep at eleven fifteen. Sofia and Mariah hauled the wet, heavy load to the dryer together, Mariah wiping out the drum while Sofia fed in the darks and the tablecloth. Sofia set the timer on her phone for fifty minutes and wrote on a sticky note in big letters: CLEAN LINT EVERY LOAD. She slapped it onto the dryer door where nobody could miss it.

By noon the darks were dry in forty-two minutes, warm and smelling like the basement's clean soap smell, and Sofia folded the tablecloth in crisp thirds the way Abuela always did. When the family crowded in, she carried it upstairs and spread it over the table, smoothing the last wrinkle with her palm as the birthday candles came out of the box.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In farsightedness, light focuses behind the retina, so near objects look blurry, and it is corrected with convex lenses.
story:
The day Ellie's glasses arrived, she carried the box to the kitchen table and opened it like it might contradict her. For weeks she had argued that the board wasn't blurry, that she was just tired, but the eye doctor had insisted, and now the evidence sat in her hands.

Last month, Ariyah had leaned across the desk in science and whispered, "You squint like it's your job." Ellie had laughed it off, but then came the flashback she couldn't shake: the headache after reading, the way she had to hold her phone at arm's length, the day she copied Miah's homework because the page swam. Her mom booked the appointment anyway.

She slid the glasses on. The world sharpened, but when she looked in the hallway mirror, she flinched. Her eyes looked huge behind the lenses, like a cartoon character's. "That's it, I'm never wearing these to school," she said out loud.

"Try this," her mom called from the couch, holding up her own reading glasses. Ellie looked over. Behind her mom's lenses, her eyes looked smaller, not bigger. Ellie frowned and pulled out her phone, texting Ariyah, who was notorious for knowing random science facts. Ariyah texted back within a minute: "what lens shape?" Ellie held each pair up to the window. Her mom's glasses curved out at the middle, thinner at the edges. Hers did too, but she remembered the doctor's chart, the one with the little diagram. She found the sheet in her backpack, still folded into her notebook's spine, and flattened it out. There it was: her lenses were convex, thicker in the middle, the kind for farsightedness, where light focuses behind the retina instead of right on it, so near objects looked blurry until the lenses fixed it.

"So mine make things look bigger," Ellie said slowly, holding her glasses up beside her mom's. "And yours make things look smaller?" Her mom shrugged. Ellie grabbed a pencil and held it behind each pair. Behind her glasses, the pencil fattened. Behind her mom's, it thinned. She tested it twice more with the pencil and once with the corner of a cereal box, and every time the result came out the same, which meant it wasn't a trick of the mirror. Her eyes looked bigger because her lenses magnified them.

The next morning she wore the glasses to school, bracing for comments. Ariyah met her at the door, squinting theatrically. "Your eyes," Ariyah said. Ellie held up a finger. "Convex lenses. Farsightedness. It's science." Miah appeared behind them, peering at her face. "They make your eyes look bigger," he said. "Mine make mine look smaller." He tapped his own frames. Ellie grinned and pushed her glasses up her nose. "Trade you for a day and find out why."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: At the Scripps National Spelling Bee, spellers may ask for a word's definition, part of speech, language of origin, or a sentence using it.
story:
The morning of the county spelling bee, Jordan boarded the school bus holding his word list like it was made of glass. He had been meticulous about studying, quizzing himself at breakfast, at lunch, even while brushing his teeth, which had led to one unfortunate incident involving toothpaste and the word "catastrophe." Adem slid into the seat beside him and peeked at the list.

"You still shaky on the ones with double letters," Adem said.

"That's the problem," Jordan said. "I can't isolate which ones are hard. They all look the same after a while." His stomach made a noise like the bus engine starting up. Somewhere behind them, Marylou was doing a victory dance because she had spelled "iridescent" correctly three times in a row.

At the middle school gym, rows of folding chairs faced a small stage with a microphone. The pronouncer, Mr. Robinson from the public library, adjusted his glasses and explained the rules. Jordan half listened until one sentence caught him like a hook.

"Spellers," Mr. Robinson said, "you may ask for the word's definition, its part of speech, its language of origin, or a sentence using it."

Wait. Language of origin? Jordan leaned forward. Could you do that? He had watched the Scripps bee on television, and now that he thought about it, the spellers up there in the bright lights were always asking questions. Language of origin. Part of speech. Why hadn't he noticed what they were doing? It was like a secret hiding in plain sight, and he had been staring right past it.

He tested the idea in his head. A word from French, like "ballet," often had its own spelling habits. If he knew where a word came from, maybe he could guess how it behaved. But did the county bee allow the same questions? Only one way to find out.

Three rounds went by. Marylou went out on "necessary," glaring at the double s like it had personally betrayed her. Adem survived "trapeze" and whispered "recession" to himself afterwards, over and over, as if practicing for a future round. Then Mr. Robinson leaned into the microphone and said, "Jordan. Your word is 'gamut.'"

Gamut. Jordan's mind went white, then flooded with wrong spellings. G-a-m... The gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn, and somewhere a basketball bounced in the hallway. He opened his mouth to guess, then stopped. Guessing was what you did when you had nothing. He had something.

"Can I have the language of origin?" he asked.

Mr. Robinson blinked, then nodded. "It comes from Latin, through Italian." A murmur went through the audience, the good kind. Italian. Latin roots, then, and Jordan knew how Latin words liked their letters arranged. The u after the m suddenly felt certain, the way a puzzle piece clicks when you stop forcing it.

"G-a-m-u-t. Gamut."

"That is correct."

Jordan sat down, heart hammering, and caught Marylou grinning at him. Later, in the final round, when he got "questionnaire" and asked for a sentence using it, he was already planning the two n's before Mr. Robinson finished saying, "The secretary lost the questionnaire in the pile on her desk."

Adem leaned over during the break. "So that's your trick? You just ask questions?"

"It's not a trick," Jordan said. "It's in the rules. I just never asked what was in there before."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The plain-folks technique presents a politician or company as ordinary, everyday people, so the audience trusts them as "one of us."
story:
Everly sat cross-legged on the living room rug with her tablet propped against a throw pillow, replaying the campaign video that the whole sixth grade had watched that morning. On screen, a boy from her class strolled through the cafeteria carrying a lunch tray exactly like everybody else's, laughed with friends, and bit into a sandwich while the words "One of Us" glowed across the bottom. Nia, sprawled on the couch with popcorn, leaned closer. "He seems so normal," she said. "I'd vote for him."

"But what's his plan?" Everly asked. She tapped pause. "He never says one thing about what he'd actually do if he won." The living room smelled like melted butter, and somewhere behind them the kitchen faucet dripped in a slow, patient rhythm. Emile, who was running against the sandwich boy and currently trailing by a mile, sat on the armrest looking miserable. "His whole video is just him eating lunch," Emile said. "That's it. That's his campaign."

Everly scrolled back and watched again, chewing a popcorn kernel she'd burned her fingers on. On the way home they had passed a shoe billboard with a famous singer's face, and a cereal commercial had claimed everyone was buying it, and the words "amazing" and "disgusting" had been doing a lot of heavy lifting in every ad she'd seen since Tuesday. Now she recognized the same tricks pointing at her. "It's the lunch tray," she said slowly. "He's showing himself like he's an ordinary, everyday kid, so we trust him as one of us. The plain-folks technique, I think it's called." Emile wrote the words on his hand with a pen, which struck Everly as a very Emile thing to do.

"So we do the same thing?" Emile asked. Everly shook her head. "We test it. We make two videos." She borrowed her dad's phone and filmed Emile in the living room, first standing stiffly reciting slogans about leadership and spirit, then a second version where he sat on the couch in his hoodie telling a short anecdote about the time he got his tie stuck in the pencil sharpener, and then, plainly, naming three things he wanted to change: longer recess, a fix for the broken water fountain, a student suggestion box. Same boy, two versions. Only one difference.

The next morning she showed both videos to Nia before homeroom, one after the other, saying nothing in between. After the first, Nia shrugged. After the second, Nia laughed at the tie story and then said, "Wait, he wants a suggestion box? Nobody's mentioned an actual idea all week. He seems way more credible than the sandwich guy." Everly felt something click into place, quiet and satisfying, like the last piece of a puzzle finding its slot.

The class voted on Friday. When Mr. Shin read out the results, Emile won by six votes, and during his victory speech he held up his hand, where the ink from Tuesday had smudged into a blue blob. "As your president," he said solemnly, "I promise to govern the pencil sharpener with great care." Nia snorted so hard her own tie flapped. Everly grinned and raised her hand. "First suggestion," she called out. "A new water fountain."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 2 of the Canadian Charter protects fundamental freedoms, including freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of association.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and pencil shavings, which Alexander figured was what democracy smelled like when it happened in a school. His mom had dragged him along to vote, and Paige and Rafael had come too because Ms. Mehta's assignment was due Monday: pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, read it, and explain it in your own words. To a classmate. Out loud. Without throwing up.

"Okay," Paige said, pacing between the folding tables. "Our plan stands. We protest the park closure on Saturday. Signs, chanting, the works. But first we need to know if we're even allowed."

Rafael peered through the door at the voters lining up. "Those people are doing rights right now. Voting. Can we ask one?"

"You want to interview a voter," Alexander said. "In the middle of voting."

"I want to interview the line. Lines precede voting. Everyone knows that."

A poll worker with a lanyard and a chronic shortage of patience shooed them away from the doorway, so they retreated to the hallway water fountain. Alexander pulled out his phone and typed charter rights into the search bar. His heart did a small drumroll. If the answer was no, the whole Saturday plan collapsed like a bad tent.

"Here," he said, reading fast. "Section 2 of the Charter protects fundamental freedoms. That's freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly, and freedom of association."

"Peaceful assembly," Paige repeated, holding up her sign sketch like a lens that had suddenly focused. "That's us! Assembling! Peacefully!"

"It says peaceful," Rafael warned. "So no megaphone screaming."

"I own one megaphone and you're ruining my dream."

"Association means we can form our group," Alexander said slowly, testing the idea against Saturday like a tongue against a wobbly tooth. "The club, the protest, all of it. It's protected. And expression covers the signs."

"Even my sign that says SAVE PINE HOLLOW PARK, YOU GOONS?"

"Especially that one."

Ms. Mehta appeared down the hall carrying a ballot box, spotted them, and raised an eyebrow. "Section 2?" she asked.

Alexander grinned. "Saturday, Pine Hollow Park, ten o'clock. Bring a sign."

She held up a piece of poster board already lettered in purple marker. "I'll precede you all there."

"TEACHERS FOR GOONS!" Rafael shouted at the ceiling, and the poll worker stuck her head out and said, "Quiet in the gym, please, democracy is trying to concentrate."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish nouns have grammatical gender, so a male dog is "el perro" and a female dog is "la perra."
story:
At his grandfather's kitchen table, Max spread out his Spanish homework and stared at the blank lines. He had to write full sentences about his family and his pets, and so far he had written exactly one word: "perro." His dog, Peanut, was asleep on the rug with her legs twitching, probably dreaming about the neighbor's cat.

"Tengo un perro," Max said out loud, and wrote it down. His grandfather looked up from his crossword.

"Peanut is not a perro," he said. "Peanut is a perra."

"A what?"

"Spanish nouns have grammatical gender. A male dog is el perro, and a female dog is la perra." His grandfather went back to his crossword, as if he had just told Max the time.

Max looked at Peanut, who was definitely female, and crossed out his sentence. So the word for dog changed depending on the dog. He tried his grandfather with a test. "What if I had a male cat?"

"El gato."

"And a female cat?"

"La gata." His grandfather raised an eyebrow. "You're going to make me do your homework."

"I'm testing a pattern," Max said. He wrote the pairs in two columns, then tried to coordinate them in sentences. "Mi abuela tiene una gata." His grandmother, who was at the sink, turned around and said the sentence back with one small correction, then laughed at something and told an anecdote about a parrot her sister used to own, a bird that learned to swear in two languages and had to be given away to a fisherman. Max didn't fully believe the parrot story, but he wrote down another sentence anyway.

The flashback came to him mid-sentence. Last summer, at the zoo, he had called a huge male peacock a "she" right in front of Zariah, and she had corrected him in front of Francois and Mr. Xu, who was chaperoning, and the three of them had laughed for the entire walk to the reptile house. Max had spent a week afterward determined to learn how to tell male animals from female ones. Now, apparently, he had to do it in Spanish too.

He wrote his last sentence about Peanut: "Mi perra es nocturna, como un búho." That part wasn't true, exactly. Peanut slept all day and all night. But his grandfather read it, snorted, and said it was the best sentence on the page.

Peanut woke up, wandered over, and stepped directly onto the homework, leaving a paw print between the two columns.

"Typical," Max said. "La perra no coopera."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: With interest compounded once a year, the balance after n years equals P x (1 + r) to the power n, where r is the yearly rate as a decimal.
story:
Hayden slid forty dollars across the counter of the student bank, a folding table outside the gym that Ms. Vogel supervised on Fridays. He had been saving since September, and now the school was offering something new: a savings account that paid interest. Two kinds, according to the flyer. Simple, and compound. He didn't know what the difference was, but he knew one thing. He needed two hundred dollars by graduation for the used skateboard in the shop window on Miller Street, and forty dollars was not going to get there by itself.

"Compound," he told Ms. Vogel, mostly because the word sounded bigger.

She prescribed no advice, only nodded and wrote his name in the ledger. "Five percent, compounded once a year. That's what the school bank does. Ask questions later if you want."

In math class the next day, Julia leaned over his notebook. "You picked compound without knowing what it is?"

"Compound sounds like it compounds," Hayden said. "That's got to be more than simple anything."

Ansh spun a calculator toward him. "Try it. Five percent is point zero five. If you start with forty bucks, after one year it's forty times one point zero five. Every year it gets multiplied by one point zero five again."

Hayden hunted for the power key, the little y-to-the-x button his older cousin, a descendant of a long line of people who read calculator manuals, had shown him once. Forty, times one point zero five, then the power key, then five, for five years. He pressed equals and held his breath while the screen blinked.

Forty-four point one zero. Julia frowned. "That's only four dollars more. After five whole years?"

"Wait." Ansh grabbed the calculator and did it the simple way, five percent of forty every year, two dollars a year, ten dollars total. "Simple gets you fifty. Compound gets you forty-four point one zero." He looked up. "Compound is worse. For that rate."

"So compound is just a fancy word for slower?" Hayden said, louder than he meant to, and the kid at the next desk snorted.

Then Julia sat back, agile with a pencil, flipping the flyer over. On the back, in small print, the school bank's rate was actually seven percent for compound accounts, not five. Hayden redid it: forty times one point zero seven to the fifth power. The screen said fifty-six point one zero. Better than simple's fifty, but still nowhere near a skateboard.

He stared at the number, then at the flyer, then at Ansh. "I need a richer plan."

"You need a job," Ansh said, and pointed out the window at the student bank table, where a sign read, help wanted, ask Ms. Vogel, pays in compound interest.

Hayden was out the door before the bell finished ringing.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: An external stylesheet is connected to a web page by a link tag with rel="stylesheet" placed inside the page's head section.
story:
Gabrielle had typed her name in giant letters at the top of her page, but the words sat stubbornly against the left edge of the screen like they were glued there. Ms. Wijaya had promised that by the end of club period, everyone's heading would float in the centre of the page, and Gabrielle wanted hers centred more than she wanted the pizza the coach had mentioned for next week.

"Mine works already," Prince announced from the next computer. His heading glowed orange and sat perfectly in the middle. "Style dot css. Eight lines. Beat that."

Gabrielle looked at her own screen. She had written the same rule, text-align: center, in a file called style.css, exactly the way the whiteboard showed it. Her page had a big heading and two paragraphs about her dog, and the CSS file sat in the same folder. Nothing had happened. She saved, refreshed, saved again. Still stuck to the left, still plain black.

"Let me see," Anaya said, leaning over. She read the code slowly, her finger hovering above the screen. "The rule's the same as Prince's. Letter for letter, I think." That was the strange part. Two identical rules, one page that obeyed and one that didn't. Gabrielle felt the back of her neck go tight, the way it did when a puzzle was hiding something from her.

She was almost ready to abandon the separate file and cram her styles onto the page itself, messy but working, when she noticed something on Prince's screen. At the top, above his heading, sat two small lines she didn't have. She scrolled up on her own file to compare. Her page started with the title. His didn't. "What's that bit?" she asked.

"Link tag," Prince said, with the casual shrug of someone who had copied it from the handout without wondering about it. He pointed at the words inside it: rel="stylesheet". "It's in the head section. Top of the page."

Gabrielle stared at her own file, and the hidden cause came into focus, like when you finally spot the dog in the puzzle picture. The styles existed. The page just had no idea they were there. The stylesheet sat in the folder like a letter never posted. From Prince's perspective it was obvious, but nobody had said it out loud, and the whiteboard only showed the CSS, not the page. She clicked at the top of her file, inside the head section, and typed the link tag with rel="stylesheet", checking each character twice.

She hit refresh. Her name swung to the centre of the screen, big and blue, exactly where it belonged. Gabrielle threw both hands up, and Anaya laughed so loudly that Ms. Wijaya looked over from the other row. "It was never linked," Gabrielle said. "The whole time, the page couldn't see the file." Prince rolled his chair over to look, then scrolled to the top of his own page and tapped the two little lines with one finger. "This," he said, "is apparently the most important two lines in the room."
